utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Take a seat. THE COURT REPORTER: I'm hearing French, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we're getting French on Channel 4. Can we get that put right, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is that all right now? It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're all right. We're in business. Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zuljevic.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Mario Cerkez's Defence, I shall be asking questions of you, and I shall ask you to answer them to the best of your recollection. I should also like to ask you, and I wish to draw your attention to one thing, to wait with your answer to my question until it has been interpreted into the official languages of the court. Also, try to speak slow enough so that the interpreters can follow you. For the record, will you please tell us your name and the year of your birth.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I am Zdravko Zuljevic. I was born on the 8th of January, 1963, in Vitez, or rather Krcevine, near Vitez. I'm a Croat by ethnicity and I am a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, which means that I have dual nationality. I completed the secondary nursing school in Travnik; after that, the faculty of veterinary medicine in Sarajevo. As of 1988, I have been working as a veterinary doctor in Travnik. As of January 1993, I have been working for the veterinary station in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, you served the former JNA in Novi Sad in 1981, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the places where I served the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you acquire any rank?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not acquire any rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are married and a father of two; two and eight, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have two daughters; Ruzica who is older, she's eight now, and Monica who is five years old now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, tell us, before and during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were a member of the HDZ, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you left it in 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Thereabouts, yes. In late 1995 I ceased being an active member and stopped actively engaging in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But while you were an active member of the HDZ, did you have a particular duty in the party?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: For awhile I was on the HDZ presidency, that is, the municipal Vitez HDZ, and a member of something, how should I call it, a municipal board of some 20 members from basic village branches and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You tell us that you left the HDZ in 1995 and now you are a member of a political party called New Croat Initiative, Nova Hrvatska Inicijativa. At the same time, you're a member of the parliament of the Central Bosnian district in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also have two brothers and two sisters, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You just told us, Mr. Zuljevic, that when you graduated in 1988 you first worked as a veterinarian in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes; that is, the veterinary station in Travnik was a complex clinic which also had several smaller offices in Novi Travnik, Vitez, Turbe, Han Bila, among other places. At first I worked in Turbe for a short time; then I was transferred to Novi Travnik, and there I worked until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, you moved to Vitez and began to work for the veterinary clinic there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, where is the building of the veterinary station in Vitez; in what part of town?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: It is in a suburb called Rijeka, at the junction of Stjepan Radica and Tima Ujevica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is the part of Vitez called Rijeka, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You lived in the same building, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As of 1991, I was allotted a flat at the veterinary clinic, but I did not move into it until late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is on the first floor and the clinic is on the ground floor, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Although you tell us that in 1992 you did not live in that building, but you nevertheless lived in Vitez, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I lived in the old part of Vitez, in another suburb with a majority Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. In 1992, Vitez was shelled on several occasions by the JNA air force. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My question is, Mr. Zuljevic, if you remember that, when fearing the air bombing, the population of Vitez went to makeshift shelters.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: That was what we did. There were very many such shelters, that is, all the cellars, all the basements of buildings were that. In suburbs and villages, certain places were designated in case of the bombing of the suburbs or, rather, urban areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the town, it was the cellars and basements of residential buildings that were used as such.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you know if the cellar of the veterinary clinic was also used as such a shelter for surrounding buildings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the basement of the veterinary station was designated by the authorities as one such shelter. In 1992, all the residents in that area, in Rijeka, came there and would spend sometimes the whole day there, right next to the veterinary clinic, in its yard sometimes. And because the alarms were very frequent, they would go down to the basement and then come out. It was a rather densely populated area and the houses were very near one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So that basement was a safe place, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: It was quite safe because it is well dug in, or rather, it is a proper cellar. The whole of it is under the ground so that it offered a very high degree of safety bar direct hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And since the time when you got the job there and joined the veterinary clinic Vitez, were you also a member of the village guards in Rijeka or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: All I did was veterinary medicine with two colleagues, or rather, one colleague, Fuad Zeco who is a Muslim, and with Cazim Patkovic who is also a Muslim. We worked at the veterinary clinic, or rather we jointly decided to start the proceedings in 1992 to single out the veterinary clinic from the veterinary station in Travnik, and in Zenica, in the higher court, we registered the Vitez clinic as a public company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you also had an opportunity, Mr. Zuljevic, that in surrounding buildings there were also village guards organised there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Such practice had existed already a year before, not only in Rijeka but also around the town. There were some organised mixed patrols involving special in the town both men of the Croat ethnicity and men of the Muslim ethnicity. This was particularly evident in villages where it was an obligatory practice, and I frequently came into contact with such armed guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who were the members of the village guards that you used to meet when you did your rounds in the villages?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the members were mostly armed civilians. Some of them had parts of uniforms, some of them did not have any uniform at all but, for the most part, they wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, let us try to recall, Mr. Zuljevic, the witnesses of the 16th of April 1993 when, in point of fact, the conflict escalated in Vitez and the nearby area. What was your experience that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, like any normal man, that is the hardest day in my life, and I have tried to suppress the memories of that, but still I again have need to remember it all. So on the 15th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't want you to stop telling us what happened, but we have a large number of witnesses this week and -- which we have to get through so we will just try and deal, if we may, with those matters which are strictly relevant. Mr. Mikulicic, what is it you want the witness to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like that witness in his own word to explain his experience on the morning of 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How is that going to help us, if you will forgive me asking? What is it you want to tell us about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is the day that the first internees were brought to the veterinary clinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is that that you want to ask him about. Yes, perhaps ask him that. Were you in the station when the detainees came?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: That morning, no, I was not at the station when the first internees arrived. But I was in a building which is very near the veterinary station because people who had been there already called me to do something in the command building of a local unit of the then Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. Perhaps it will be better if I ask you questions and thus take you through your evidence. Is it true that early in the morning when you heard the gunfire, you noticed a rather large group of people arrive to that area where you were, to the area of Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, after the first shots, or after the neighbours banged on my door and woke me up, they told me that very intensive gunfire had started and invited me to come out with my wife and my children, or rather one child because at that time I only had one child which was 10 months old, and that I should go to the command building and to be issued orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You tell us that in the building of Sumarija, there was the commander of a local unit of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you observe that larger group of people began to gather there which did not come from that part of the town originally?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time the chaos had already begun on the road passing the -- by the Sumarija and people were arriving in groups. They were fleeing into town, others were fleeing from the town. There was a chaos, and I recognised a man in the group who used to work at the local slaughter house and his name was Stipo Jukic. He was an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, what village did he come from?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: He lived on the boundary between the village of Gornja Dubravica and Poculica. That is the first house, one could say, in the village of Poculica right next to the so-called elevation called Vrhivcica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why did that man tell you -- why did he come and other people? Why did they come from Poculica to the building of Sumarija?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were on their way to the town, but he came there to seek help because he was an elderly man and he was frightened and weeping. He said to the doctor, They set my house on fire. I barely managed to flee into the woods, or rather, towards the stream. And then they asked assistance to be put up somewhere, and then they were directed into town, I suppose. Some civilian organisation took care of them, I suppose, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that man from Poculica, did he tell you who had attacked their village and set his house on fire?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that it was his neighbours who had done that of Muslim ethnicity. That is Bosniak now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said your neighbour came to wake you up. What is his name?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: His name is Rajko Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And he warned you that you should take your family to a safer place and offered you his own flat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His flat was also not far from Sumarija, and as my wife and his wife spent all day in the shelter, the two of them were much closer than the two of us were. And when I asked, well, where should I take my wife and child, he said, well, I could go to my wife, Mada, and told me to come to the Sumarija building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you went to the Sumarija building then. When you got there, what did they tell you? Who did you find when you got there, and what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived, there was Rajko and some other young men whom I knew by sight from the neighbourhood. There was -- that is to say, a little later, Mr. Bertovic turned up whom I didn't know either by name or by sight. I got to know that he would be the commander of that local unit later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you came to understand that you arrived into a building where there was a command present and later on you learned that the commanding officer there was this man named Bertovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what were you told was your task, Mr. Zuljevic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: They told me that I was to go into the room where the medicines were, that was a smaller room with a cupboard with all the sanitary material and medicines, and that together with Dr. Pocrnja, from that day on, I would be in charge of this sort of outpatient's department in the Sumarija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who is Dr. Pocrnja, please tell us, Mr. Zuljevic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pocrnja was from Vitez. He was a gynecologist, in fact, but according to his wartime reserve assignment, in case of war, he was assigned to a little clinic of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But what actually happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pocrnja, in fact one or two days previously, had left for Zenica and the morning found him in Zenica so he was not able to take up his assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, when you came to the Sumarija building and when you were told of your assignments by the commanding officer, that actually meant that you were being mobilised for the purposes of the military unit; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And from that day on, I was issued a certificate stating that I had, in fact, being mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On that particular morning when you were informed with your assignments and tasks orally, did you receive a document of any kind stipulating that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I received no document whatsoever at that time, it was just an oral information given to me that I was assigned the work that I had been assigned to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So as Dr. Pocrnja was cut off in Zenica, you were the head of this makeshift clinic and were able to give out first aid to the wounded and injured population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you do this for the purposes of the soldiers or for civilians as well?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, both for soldiers and civilians alike regardless of who was injured or wounded or needed attention, regardless of what ethnicity or whatever. I was there to tend to all the people in the building, around the building, and on the terrain in general, in the field in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On that particular day or around that time, were you called to give medical help, called to the building of the veterinary station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was called. One of the people who were internees was an elderly man and he said he suffered from kidney problems, that he had problems urinating and was in great pain when he had to urinate and that he felt generally sick. I talked to his son, whom I knew, and his name was Sejo Zecovic. So his father, the sick man, was Camil Zecovic. I went off, that is to say, I returned to the clinic, found the medicines he needed, diuretics for the most part, and analgesics, and I said that he ought to go home, which was in the vicinity, go back to his own house because it was fairly cold. And it would be a good idea if he could get warm, have some hot tea to drink, and spend time in his own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, we'll come back to that later on. But let me go on to ask you the following: When you arrived at the veterinary station where you worked, what did you notice, that is to say, at the entrance to the building, at the entrance door?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I noticed that the door had been forcibly opened and that there were a number of men in the station of all ages, conscripts, mostly. And I can say with full responsibility that they moved around freely, that is to say, around the building, in the courtyard and in the building as well. There were people that were coming and going from the basement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. According to your assessment, how many men would you say there were at that particular time in the veterinary station building?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to give you an exact number, but I would say there might have been 50 to 60 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Did you have occasion to see anybody bringing these people into the veterinary station? Were they brought there by anybody?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't see them actually being brought in, but I did see that they were there, and that later in the course of the day, other people were brought there too who had either passed by the street or whatever. And I saw people near to Darko Kraljevic's house who were members of what was that unit called, the Special Purposes Unit, the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who ordered those people to be brought to the veterinary station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that these people moved around freely both in the building and around the building itself. Can you tell us whether you noticed that they were guarded in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: There was a sort of guard, we could call it that. They were also guys from the neighbourhood, but they spoke openly to them. There were no conflicts, there was no maltreatment, and in the first couple of days, they were still able to use the telephone which was still connected in the veterinary station. Their wives could bring them in drink, and they came to see how they were, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you noticed that these people were being guarded by some guys from the neighbourhood. Were they the ones you'd referred to earlier on as members of the village guard, or were they uniformed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I think they were guys from the village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During your visit to the veterinary station, did you happen to see anybody maltreating those individuals, physically abusing them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not notice anything like that. I knew five or six people who were there. I talked to them and they didn't complain of anything like that. They were just afraid, and they said, "Doctor, can you help us? What's going on?" As far as I was able to, I said that I would help them, that I was there to help them and I would stop by later on. I brought my colleague, Mr. Zeco, some aspirin that he needed. Dr. Zubar helped me come by those aspirins in the central chemistry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, 17th, and 18th, was there shelling and shooting in town?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: There was -- that is to say, the shooting got stronger, and the shelling did in particular. Lots of people came seeking help. It was generally a chaotic situation, lots of confusion. People were in shock, under stress. They asked for tranquilisers. They couldn't take these sudden changes and frustrations. I think the situation, generally speaking, was very chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Thank you. When you talked to these people in the veterinary station, did you notice any of them having visible physical injuries of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you ever forced to give medical aid, as in bandage wounds, for injuries of this kind?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I never gave medical assistance for this kind of injury to people at the veterinary station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, if I understand you properly, the only more serious intervention was to that kidney patient, Mr. Camil Zecevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: According to your recollections, how long were those people in and around the veterinary station? How long did they stay there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that they were there between four and six days. I can't say exactly because I had other duties to perform; I had to go out into the field. Actually, later on there was no need for me to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, or did you happen to hear where they were transferred to after the veterinary station? Where were they taken?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember on one occasion returning from pulling out a soldier from the front line between Kruscica and Rijeka who was shot through the pelvis and we had to see to him, I went to in front of the Sumarija building and I was told that the internees had been transferred to the primary school in Donja Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, you had no further contact with those people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Over the next few days that they stayed there I had no further contact with them. But when they returned home, we had occasion to talk again, and I was in contact with them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So after they returned, after they left the school, did they complain of their treatment there? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that they were a little afraid and rather reserved, so we didn't actually discuss that topic much. I spent most of my time with one particular family, that is to say, the family of Camil Zecevic, his two sons, his young bride, and their children. We were neighbours, we would sit around drinking coffee, and I did what I could to calm them, to give them back their self-confidence and to say that everything would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. So, Mr. Zuljevic, when the conflict broke out, during that first stage you actually gave medical assistance to the population at large; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, at the end of that month, at the end of April, you received a call. Could you tell us briefly what all that was about?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan Skopljak called me; that is to say, he sent people from the police who were put up in the police building in Vitez, two policemen, that is, who told me that Marijan was looking for me, wanted to see me, and that I should go to the police building. I was in my own apartment at the time; I was having a shower, I think. I left immediately; I was still wet but I left immediately and waited in the police building, and he did not turn up. Then I asked them to explain why I had been brought there and when Marijan Skopljak would turn up. He was attending a meeting in the post office building, and I left demonstratively and went to the PTT building myself. He told me to sit down, said that I would be given some assignments which I was to perform from there on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. At that time did you know what function Marijan Skopljak had?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I think he was head of the defence department attached to the HVO or attached to the municipality. I don't know in any greater detail what his actual job was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you complained about this kind of conduct, the fact that he had sent two policemen. But then he gave you oral instructions as to your further duties and assignments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Marijan Skopljak told me that I should go and find Mr. Marko Strbac, who was the director up until that time of the state agricultural company, the livestock farm. He said that together with him and someone from the civil defence department I should organise rounding up the livestock that was freely roaming the fields, and that we should take the livestock, the cattle, to the SPS building which was located on the other side of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That agricultural concern, the farm that was in Vitez and which had a certain number of cattle, of livestock, after the conflict broke out, who supervised the farm? Which armed force supervised the farm?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on that very first day, within the farm compound and the main building, which was next to a large Muslim village named Grbavica, members of the BH army entered and they rounded up some of the cattle for slaughter; whereas, the cows that were being milked were sent to Viteska Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So you executed your duty and organised the rounding up of this cattle and cows, and you rounded them up into the SPS factory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After having performed that assignment, what other assignments did you receive?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: They told me that over the next few days I should stay put at the SPS and that we should examine the cattle to see which of the cows were pregnant and needed special care and attention, and that we were to find people to feed the cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from Marijan Skopljak, whom you said was the head of the defence department, you were given your wartime assignment, is that right, within the frameworks of your professional training?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you for the purposes of which military unit you were doing that work?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't specify the unit or the conditions that I was to work under. He just told me what my work was to be. So when we completed this assignment, I was told - that is to say, some 20 days went by, perhaps a month went by after I had performed this assignment with the cattle - that I should contact Vlado Alilovic, I think that was his name, and that we should see to the rest of the livestock and to buying up the livestock; that is to say, that we should buy up the livestock that could serve as food for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So your job was, in fact, to control the food distributed to the military units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After these makeshift kitchens were set up, field kitchens for the units which existed in every village for the village unit, I would tour the slaughterhouses, makeshift slaughterhouses, and then I would tour the kitchens as well to see that the minimum hygiene standards were adhered to. We tried to find disinfectants and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were you also issued with a uniform and weapons, since you were now part of the military?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Before the escalation of the Croat-Muslim conflict and throughout the whole war, I never wore a uniform nor was I armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But is it true that after the end of the war and the signing of the ceasefire, you were given the status of a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was given this status as a member of the Vitez Brigade. Perhaps I should say that after Mr. Juric became commander, an attempt was made to put in order all these positions in the brigade, and I was issued with a decision saying that I was the head of the veterinary service at the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What time was this; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was considerably later. It was when Juric -- when Mario was replaced and Juric took over the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your membership in the HVO, you gained the right to a certificate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever manage to exercise this right or, rather, to make use of these certificates?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Neither I nor about 70 per cent of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of their ethnicity, will be able to make use of these certificates. I think that this is actually a trick to trick ordinary citizens who actually cannot make use of these certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, let us now pass on to another topic which is somewhat different from this. You said that you lived in the building of the veterinary station and that this was the part of Vitez called Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the building of the veterinary station, was there also a family house belonging to Darko Kraljevic and his family?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, his family house was there and the family house of his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far, approximately, was Darko Kraljevic's house from the building of the veterinary station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not more than 100, 120, 130; 150 metres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you associate with Darko Kraljevic or have any personal contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic was not among the people I kept company with. We did not know one another personally or have any personal contacts, although I knew him because -- well, I knew him by sight but we never said Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you know what his role was in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that Darko Kraljevic led a unit as far back as 1992, and that from time to time he went to the Vlasic plateau to perform some military operations, which I thought were very adventurous, in the area of Turbe, attacking in the direction of Turbe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice the members of the unit Vitezovi gathering around his house near the veterinary station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a way, they gathered. This was the place where they gathered, and a group of I don't know how many people could always be seen in front of his house. They were armed and they made a lot of noise. I think they drank. They fired shots and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see, among the men gathering around Darko Kraljevic's house, did you ever see Mario Cerkez among them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not notice Cerkez coming to Darko Kraljevic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see the two of them together keeping company together?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I was never with Mario Cerkez or any of the commanders. So until the beginning of the conflict, I worked at the veterinary station, and I spent most of the time in the station or around it. I rarely went to town except when I went to the SPS or if I had to go and provide medical assistance in a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for Darko Kraljevic, you mentioned that he was an adventurer. How would you describe him? Was he part of a military hierarchy? Did anyone issue him orders? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I think he did not take orders from anyone. He had his own men independently. As far as I could see, the men who were in his unit changed very often. Some men went, others came. It was not a well-organised military unit. There were no standards that were maintained. They fired shots on their way back from the battlefield. They were drunk. They were men who frightened their neighbours, whether they were Croats, Muslims or Serbs. They frightened them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, did you notice there were Muslim young men in his unit?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, one could say I saw a few men of Muslim ethnicity who came to Darko's house and who kept company with him throughout the war and after the war, and who were in Vitez the whole time. One of these young men is still in Vitez. I don't know his name, but he goes by the name of Bagrem, that's his nickname. And another young man whose name was Nedim and his nickname was "Nedo." And there may be others but I didn't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said at the beginning of your testimony, Mr. Zuljevic, that in the Rijeka area in Vitez, the population was mixed, there were Muslim houses, Croatian houses, in blocks of flats that tenants were mixed. After the war, after the internees came back from the Dubravica primary school, did anyone maltreat them in their homes, try to drive them out? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not see that, but it's possible such things happened that certain individuals, people who had been expelled from their own homes and were wandering about without a place to stay, that those people exerted pressure. For example, my next door neighbour, Camil Zecovic, remained there throughout this time, and it's true that someone came and moved into part of his house, and Camil later went to stay with another neighbour, a Muslim, and then after that he went back to his own house. There were other people, for example, the Ugarak family, several Tuca family members who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. While there were seven or eight families who stayed and lived in that area, did you notice humanitarian aid being given to those people?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid, as much as we received, was distributed equally. Later we went into town to get humanitarian aid from the Red Cross and other international organisations, and these people were given this aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of any discrimination against citizens of Muslim ethnicity as far as the distribution of aid was concerned or the provision of medical assistance and other sorts of welfare for the population?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't say as regards the distribution of humanitarian aid, which was very scarce, I can't say that it was fair. I think it was not fair even among the Croats. And there was discrimination because there was no aid or rather there was no discrimination in the sense that no one would be given any aid at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, throughout this time while you were in the military part of the HVO, did you ever see, hear, or experience an order which would be designed to discriminate against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard such an order, nor was I ever in a position to hear such an order being issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your responses. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Your Honours, if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, allow me to introduce myself again. My name is Mirko Naumovski, I am a lawyer from Zagreb, and together with Mr. Stephen Sayers, I am Defence counsel for Dario Kordic. I will ask you just a few questions. At the end of April, after you started performing veterinary duties in the brigade, you often toured the area to supervise slaughterhouses, kitchens and so on. That was part of your job.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, as a veterinarian, did you have to take care of the livestock belonging to the refugees who came from Travnik in June 1993 and some of them brought their cattle with them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was part of our task, yes, among other things. All the stray livestock or wounded livestock was taken to the SPS compound, and wounded cattle wounded by bullets or shells were slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And making the rounds, did you notice a large number of refugees arriving in Vitez in June?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, up until the end of June, there was heavy fighting in the surrounding villages and people came all the time. Then they would go back if the lines shifted. So they would go back to their homes, and they would come and go. There were a lot of people who brought their cattle from Nova Bila, and that was in May or June, the end of May, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I assume that these refugees exerted pressure on the local population. You mentioned the example of your neighbour, Camil Zecovic, that someone had moved into his house. I assume it was one of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was pressure, if I may say, it seems to me that the whole point of the fighting in Vitez and the Lasva river valley was to have a large number of refugees in this small area. They came from Sandzak, from Republica Srpska, from Jajce, from Dobratici, from the Vlasic plateau and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time that we are talking about in June, I assume that you know -- or rather, do you know that on the 10th of June 1993, a shell fell on a playground where some children were playing and eight children were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that, and I know some of the parents of these children who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And this event of the 10th of June in the evening, did it cause further indignation among the local people and the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, people were killed every day, not just one or two, but more than that, regularly. But, of course, the death of children, of innocent children, caused more indignation than usual. People were very upset, especially women, mothers, and they came to the command and to the Sumarija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zuljevic, would you tell us, at this time, did you know when you were making the rounds, did you see parts of the Tuzla convoy, the Convoy of Joy as it is called in our case, which arrived on the 11th of June in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I can say something about this. I was on my way back from the village of Male Mosunj. I had my bike. My family was accommodated there later on. I was going back to Vitez, and I saw the remains of the convoy. I saw trucks that had turned over, that had fallen into ditches. I saw some children taking gasoline out of a tank truck in pails and taking it to their homes. I saw people carrying clothing and, because the main road was blocked, I came to the town. I was very upset, and I went to see Mr. Ivica Santic and I said to him, "Ivica, can you not put an end to this shame? Look at what the people in the villages are doing." And he said, "I've done everything I could. I did my best. I sent the police but there's general chaos and no one can control the events surrounding the convoy."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can clarify two details. You were upset because of the looting of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a human being, I was very indignant about what was being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And Mr. Ivica Santic to whom you were applied, was he the mayor of Vitez then?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was then the official mayor of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, from what you saw in the field and from this conversation, can it be concluded that what you saw was chaotic situation, was anarchy beyond control, or do you think it was the result of an organised action to loot the convoy?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was a chaotic situation. It was anarchic, even more than that. If I could find a stronger word I would use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Dario Kordic having anything to do with the stopping of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And one more question, Mr. Zuljevic: Making your rounds as a veterinarian, and you went all over the area, did you ever see any units of the Croatian army in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. There were no such units in Vitez or around it ever. I can say that there was a unit in 1992 from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I never saw any trace of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Zuljevic. Your Honours, I have completed my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are not, I think, an expert on the Vitezovi and Darko Kraljevic, are you, Mr. Zuljevic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I am a veterinarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't know the detail of any orders that Darko Kraljevic received or gave?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't know to what degree he coordinated the activities of his group with other groups operating in the area of Vitez, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: At such meetings or in command at such sessions, I wasn't present there so that I can't tell you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was, of course, pursuing, broadly speaking, Croatian objectives at the very least; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: And which were Darko Kraljevic's objectives, I really can't say. But to my mind, I am a Croat. But those were not my Croat objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked about Dario Kordic by his counsel. By the way, did you speak to his counsel before giving evidence here?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke with Mr. Naumovski for about five minutes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Kordic at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Kordic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long for?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Not long. We met in 1991 and we were together on various occasions and spent some time together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Including in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: 1991, and perhaps in 1992 too. I'm not sure but, yes, we used to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you meet him about political matters?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Darko was an HDZ member and I was also an HDZ member so that was to discuss political matters that we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You referred to Darko. Are you referring to Dario Kordic or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dario, Dario Kordic. I'm sorry, Darko, Dario, it's the same name with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you last meet him in relation to political matters, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, early 1992 could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And after that, when he became a senior politician in the area, you had no contact with him; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you can't tell us anything of what he was doing in late 1992 or in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything because I no longer had the opportunity of being in such a political company. My functions as a political member did not go beyond the local level so that we stopped seeing each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You spoke of Ivica Santic who you spoke to at the time of the convoy. How well did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Ivica Santic as a politician in the HDZ too, as a man who was one of the founders of that political party. I know him from the electoral period when the first elections were held and when Ivica Santic became the head of the municipality. And so I know him. We met more often and saw one another more often because, being the municipal head, he also took care of agriculture and would frequently seek my advice on various professional matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So as a person -- or sorry, where is Mr. Santic now?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: For the -- I did not see him these last two or three months, but I sometimes see him in Vitez. We sit down to a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so far as you understand, he's still in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that for the past two or three months I have not seen him, so he could be in Vitez still, but perhaps he is not. I cannot really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So of course his position as mayor would enable him to know fully what was going on in Vitez in the first half of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is how it should be were it a normal peaceful situation. But 1992 and the former half of 1993 were the period when anarchy began to set in, lack of authority. The state did not function and Ivica Santic or any other mayor had any contact with any superior authorities, state authorities. So that whenever something happened -- rather all problems of the state were being solved in an area, in a dismembered area. The Croat people and people of Muslim origin who were responsible for politics had some meetings, had some talks, but they also had some reserve policies. They were receiving -- or it seems to me -- well, in any event, they did not show much readiness, nor could they really get all the information and organise the civilian life as it should be organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the answer to my question could be more shortly put. Of all people in Vitez, Ivica Santic should know pretty much the detail of what was going on; that would be correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: If he had such an opportunity, if he was receiving information, and he was strong enough, then, yes, that is how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Santic trust you to the degree that he told you things that he'd heard and things that he'd done as a politician?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I mean, Santic and I, we were acquaintances but we were not friends, nor were we together all that often to discuss that. When he was the mayor, I was the veterinarian; I went about my business and he went about his. So some more profound analysis, no, we never discussed those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the events of the 15th, 16th of April were the turning point for Vitez, as for so many other municipalities in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know whether the 15th and the 16th were the turning point. I think that the cart started downhill, if I may put it that way, much earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take you through all of the history of Vitez because you've only come here to give evidence on some narrowish points. But you have told us you were moving at the local political level. If that doesn't meaning speaking with Ivica Santic, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: With Ivica Santic, I talked -- I can tell you what we talked about. He would frequently call me to see how to resolve the problem of the cattle farm which was about to collapse. We even got in touch with an American humanitarian organisation which tried to help our farm. They provided us with some resources, with some feed, and I calculated how much it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to go into detail about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Santic tell you anything about a plan to have an all-out attack on Muslims on the 16th of April? Not necessarily his plan but a plan of which he was aware; did he tell you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, he never spoke to me about such matters. We never talked about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he speak at all about efforts made to get Kordic to agree to a postponement of such a plan, or postponement of an attack?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about such a plan. So of course he could not talk to me about it or discuss a plan since there was no plan, nor did I know anything about such a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at the geography, please. I haven't got very many questions to ask you. If we can go back, please, to plan 2271 and if you would place it on there. Mr. Zuljevic, are you happy dealing with plans and maps? Some people are; some people aren't. There's no criticism for those who aren't.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I think I can find my way about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What we can see on this plan, just to bring life to your evidence -- if we have it a little bit further down, or move the map up a bit, please -- move the map up a bit. No, the other way. Rijeka. There's Rijeka right at the bottom of the plan, south of the bend in the road that goes from Vitez, as the main road goes round to Dubravica and so on. You've spoken in your evidence of having to go to the SPS factory. Just remind the Judges, please, where that was, or the area of the SPS factory.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: The SPS factory is here, between Gacice and Donja Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke of the cattle there being near to Grbavica, although it's not shown on this map, the area of Grbavica is to the north of that area, near Divjak. And we've heard about how that area was in Muslim control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite. You can see Divjak, and you can even see where the farm at Divjak was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So apart from the occasion when you had to pass through to the west of Vitez to be in the area of the factory in Grbavica, you were always in Rijeka; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Not Rijeka. I went to Krcevine, I went to Gacice, Mosunj, Nova Bila; that is, I also lent regular veterinarian services during the war, not only being part of the military veterinarian services. I continued rendering these services to farmers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's have a quick look at a photograph, 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to hold it -- put it on the ELMO in the north/south way, although the photograph was taken in a different orientation, which will mean having it like that, then I think it will match what we see in the map, I think. No, I think the other way up -- no, absolutely right. The usher is right, I'm wrong. Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That shows, doesn't it, pretty well to the left of centre, the area of Rijeka? And we can see that on the other side of the road, there is very little in the way of residential habitation, that it's mostly fields; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's turn to what you say happened at the veterinary station. You say that you're not aware of any orders of a discriminatory nature. Can you tell us, then, please, why Muslim men were arrested and detained in the veterinary station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Why? I cannot say, because I neither took such decisions nor enforced them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: But that also happened on a large scale in other places, and it is a fact that it happened in Rijeka too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. So since this was an action against Muslims, you're quite unable to say whether it was or wasn't discriminatory in intention because you have no idea why it happened. That's your evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I have already said, I already described what I had seen or heard when I was answering the questions of Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard from a witness called Fuad Zeco; do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Fuad Zeco, I know him. We worked together until about the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anything that you know about this man that would mean we should doubt what he tells us, or does he appear to you to be an entirely decent and honourable man?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I know Fuad Zeco as a veterinarian, ever since I was a child, and we worked for the same company since 1988. Whether he's an honest, an honourable man, perhaps it's not for me to say anything about this, because he was my colleague. As every man, he had his ups and downs. I know that he was a man who liked to gamble.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. But apart from that, which is not, I think, a crime, is there anything you know to his detriment?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: From our conversations. For instance, we last worked together on the 15th of April, 1993. We would partake of morning coffee regularly at a nearby coffee shop at Rijeka, and naturally we also talked about politics, because for about a couple of months before that we tried, the two of us, and some other people at the veterinarian station, to put an end to this irrational trend, to try to put some common sense into people. And I tried to talk to him. I know he was a member of some Crisis Staff or, rather, of the Muslim side, so to speak, authority in Vitez. I know that even before that he told me that he went to visit the positions of the BH army on surrounding hills; he did not tell me exactly where. But I know that he had a heart condition, and he told me that he also suffered an attack because he had to climb a hill to see the positions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. I just want to be quite sure, Mr. Zuljevic, before I tell you what Mr. Zeco has told us, that there's nothing you want to say adverse to his honesty, as I understand it, and there's nothing that you're pointing to; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Was Zeco sincere or was he tendentious, I cannot tell you in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't know the circumstances in which people were taken to the veterinary centre because you weren't there. You'd just arrived and found the door broken down.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We heard that some 70 people from Rijeka were detained there. You don't challenge that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I've said, I should say 50 or 60, but they were not all from Rijeka. I knew only some of those people. There were also some whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. The man Krunoslav Bonic, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I know some Bonics. No, I did not know Krunoslav Bonic. I mean, I lived there not more than three or four months, in that locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Did you know that at the veterinary detention centre a man called Zeljko Matkovic and Krunoslav Bonic were amongst those who were controlling things? Both members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Zeljko Matkovic, and that day I saw him move around within Sumarija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. So if we've been told that he was the person principally responsible for the prisoners, you wouldn't disagree.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe not. I cannot say that he was responsible or that he was not responsible because I do not have such information available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we've been told that he got his orders from Karlo Grabovac in the forestry administration building, again, do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I was not in the room or in the command with Karlo Grabovac, so I do not know what Karlo Grabovac ordered and if he ordered anything to Mr. Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can perhaps just put the map back to remind the Judges of the geography, remind us all of the geography, if you would be so good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While I'm doing that, you weren't continuously at the veterinary centre or anything like it because you had other duties to perform; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, if we look at the map, we can see that just south of Rijeka - not too far out because we need it there - there's the area of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Trenches were dug in the area of Rijeka and Kruscica and they were dug by people who had been detained at the veterinary centre; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know who dug the trenches or where they were dug.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't know one way or another whether they were dug under terms of force; that is to say, the prisoners were forced to dig the trenches. You can't help with that, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot, no, in any greater detail. But that doesn't mean that there were not such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the deaths of two people in those areas digging trenches, Jusuf Ibrakovic and Nesib Hurem? I'm not going to produce their death certificates unless anybody wants me to. They are 2210.4 and 2210.5. Do you know anything about those two men?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not know those two men, nor did I know that they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know a man called Borislav Jozic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Borislav Jozic. He was my secondary school teacher at the medical school in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to look at possibly the only document I may trouble this witness with, see if he can help us. 734.1, it would be a new document, just look at this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just if we can be informed if that was a new document and why we were not given that document earlier if it is a new one. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It certainly is a new document. As far as I know, it's just come into my possession. It's a Zagreb document, and if it hasn't been provided to Mr. Naumovski by Zagreb, it would only be our duty to provide it under the usual terms of disclosure, but I've got things to say about documents later on today generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you would be good enough to look at original of this as we follow it in English on the overhead projector. This is a document dated the 19th of April coming from Cerkez appointing to a committee for the supervising the truce of the exchange of prisoners, Borislav Jozic, a member of the mixed committee for the truce. Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know the duties of Mr. Jozic. I saw him once or twice, perhaps, during the war, that is in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well then, if I can explain the relevance of the document rather than going through the paper chase. The document 591 which is the list of Muslim detainees spoken of by the witness Morsink and of course headed Viteska Brigade was provided to him which by the man Borislav Jozic. I ask for that document to be admitted but that's its significance and, in light of this witness' answers, I'm not going to take it any further with him. Your Honour, if you will give me a couple of minutes, I think we can conclude this witness by the break which will probably be to the Court's -- would be something the Court would prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one question about the Convoy of Joy. You have no knowledge, one way or another, whether the stopping of the convoy was organised or not, do you, because you weren't there to see how the first stopping was done. You weren't there to see who was doing it.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not have any exact information about it except what I saw with my own eyes. What people did, what citizens did, what children did, I did see that. Whether it was organised, whether it was not organised, I do not think -- I think it was just stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about 25 tonnes of humanitarian aid that we've been told was delivered to Vitez in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the circumstances of the attacks on Ahmici and the surrounding villages; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about attacks, possibly from what Ivica Santic might have told you? Do you know anything about attacks on places, is it Barin Gaj? Do you know that place?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I know the place, but I did not discuss this place, nor did Ivica Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Santic tell me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know the about the attacks on Sljivcica?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that you were given a document recognising your HVO status dated as from when, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that was the 16th of April, 1993 until -- I'm not sure, January and February 1996, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't have the documents so I can't deal with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zuljevic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, there are one or two matters. The first is this, that tomorrow morning, Judge Robinson has a hospital appointment and so we intend, under the usual Rule, to sit two Judges tomorrow morning. If there are any objections, they can be made. For the rest of the week, it is a truncated week because there are a number of matters. Wednesday afternoon, there is an additional plenary which the Judges have to attend, but we propose to sit a longer day, start at 9.15 and end at half past one, with suitable breaks. Friday we are not sitting, the Court is dealing with another case that day. Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, so that's today, tomorrow and on Thursday, we will sit a little later to try and accommodate the witnesses in order to try and get through the list. Today, we will sit until 5 o’clock but there may be changes later in the week. We'll have a break at just before 4 o’clock. You wanted to mention something about --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The documents. I think it will take me about five minutes to explain, so I can do it now or at some other time convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Some other time during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think the next witness will be one with whom I'm going to spend very much time. And it may be that what looks like a tight week for witnesses may be one we will be able to accommodate comparatively easily. We don't have the summary for the witness Badrov, and we're certainly going reach him this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt that can be provided. We'll adjourn now. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if the witness would stand, please, and take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Franjic.

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I shall be putting questions to you on behalf of the Cerkez Defence and I should like you to answer them according to the best of your recollections. I should also like to ask you to speak as slowly as possible and to make pauses between my question and your answers to help the interpreters. For purposes of the record, would you please give us your full name and date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: My name is Franjo Franjic. I was born on the 8th of April, 1950 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are a Croat by nationality of the Roman Catholic faith; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but also of the Republic of Croatia, are you not?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You completed secondary commercial school in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you are an economist by profession; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, you are now retired. You are not working anymore; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand, you shall be receiving invalidity pension as a consequence of your being injured during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You served in the former JNA in 1971 in Bileca, did you not?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after doing your military service, you were given the rank of reserve second lieutenant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are married and you have four children and three grandchildren; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are not a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have three sisters and one brother?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, having completed your schooling, did you get a job?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us where.

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: After I completed my education, I got a job in the Vjetrenica commercial enterprise where I worked until 1985, and in 1985 I went to work in Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. And from 1985 onwards, that is to say up until those unfortunate events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you worked in the Republic of Austria, did you not?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Franjic, as far as you knew, were you an isolated case or were there many people who, from your region, went to work abroad?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: There were lots of people who went to work abroad from my region and there were also those who stayed in the area when the unfortunate events took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But when you worked in Austria, you would come to your native village, would you not?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I would come for the Christmas holidays and for the Easter holidays and other holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the name of your native village is Donja Dubravica, is it not?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Let me put you right there. My native village is Donja Veceriska but I live in the village of Donja Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Donja Dubravica is, in fact, a part of Krizancevo Selo, is it not?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask the usher to put a map on the ELMO. It is Z2271, and I should like to ask the witness to show us the location of the village in which he lived exactly, that is to say, the village of Donja Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: This is Sivrino Selo, this is the road, and it is in this corner here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is the village which is north of the main road leading from Vitez to Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: From Vitez to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I beg your pardon. To Zenica via Vjetrenica. Tell us, Mr. Franjic, and I should like to ask the usher to leave the map on the ELMO because we are going to refer back to it. Tell us, please, Mr. Franjic, what was the composition, ethnically speaking, of the village in which you lived, the village of Donja Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: The ethnic composition was mixed. There were Muslims, Croats, but it was a predominantly Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Although you didn't live in the village all the time, you did come back to it from time to time and you were able to see, to observe the relationships between the Croats and the Muslims in your village?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I would come for the Easter holidays, for instance, I noticed that the situation was already tense between the Muslims and the Croats because there were mono-ethnic guards in front of houses set up to protect the families and the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As you have mentioned the Easter holidays, which year are you thinking about?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Prior to that, I assume you went back home to your native village for Christmas of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that in that period, that is to say, from the Christmas of 1992 up until Easter 1993, that relations had deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: FRANO FRANJIC
