utterances.text: Did any of them say that something might happen the next day?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was a normal evening in the disco.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I assume you were there with young people, people of your own age.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What route did you take when you drove home? Where did you start from and where were you to arrive?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, near the bus station, through Mahala, over the bridge, and then towards Krcevine. That was the road I always took.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In passing through Mahala, did you notice anything, anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I met 10 or 15 armed men near the fire station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What army did these men belong to?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They belonged to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What led you to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that part is lit up, because the road is two or three metres away, and I knew quite a few of those men there, so I knew who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where did you see them in Mahala? Can you describe the spot?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's where the fire station is. It's right next to the road. They tried to stop me; that's why I remember it so well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you stop?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. When two or three set out toward the road, they were Muslims from Kruscica, one of them stopped them and said, "Let him through."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this Beso from Kruscica was a neighbour of yours?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was from Kruscica, but we knew each other. We talked about motorcycles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you had a hobby in common.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you were not stopped. They gave a signal that you could continue.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You went home and you went to bed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before you went to bed, or when you arrived in Krcevine, did anyone say that there was any information that something might happen the next day?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. No one said anything. I even came across the village guards but said nothing. They didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were the village guards in their usual place?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were they reinforced? Were there more of them?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps this group of men belonging to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina whom you encountered in Mahala, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were they armed in the usual way or better or worse?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some of them had long artillery pieces, others had pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your village at that time, how were the village guards armed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was mostly hunting rifles, M-48s and so on. It was quite badly armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Whose weapons did people use? Who owned the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were mostly private weapons belonging to people in the guards. It was mostly hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did every member of the village guards have a weapon or did they use the same weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the same weapons were left for the next person to take up when someone went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And ethnically speaking, the village of Krcevine was what?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: A mixed one, but the Croats were a majority, however, there were also Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as for the share of Muslims and Croats, could you roughly tell us what the ratio was?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were about 10 or 15 Muslim houses and in the village Grabak, which is above Krcevine, there were some 10 or 15 Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just explaining, Grabak is just a little higher than your village.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it has a boundary, it's adjacent to us but we call it a separate village, Grabak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it is the part of the village which has its own name.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And at that time on the eve of the conflict, all three peoples lived in the village?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No; Serbs had left before. After the air bombing of Princip and others, they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But they left of their own will?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The Serbs were the majority. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did anyone force the Serbs in your village to leave or was it their decision?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was their decision. We were on very good terms both with Muslims and Serbs in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And perhaps to round off this subject, do you remember any incident, I mean an ethnic incident, an incident involving Serbs and Croats perhaps before they left?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the morning of the 16th of April, how did you wake up?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was woken up by the gunfire so I went out and saw that the fire was on Ravni Put where otherwise the village guards were told to gather. So I got up, dressed, and went to Ravni Put which is the top of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that place at Ravni Put was to be the -- was designated as a meeting point for the village guards and that was so as of the beginning of the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is at that time when the threats and some bombing by the JNA aviation started?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because Serbs were at Grabak and -- well, that was simply our meeting place; we had agreed about that it was nearest to all of us and accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That part of the village which you call Ravni Put, in terms of altitude, it is slightly higher, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you command your view of the village, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not the whole village but you can see a part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And from that place, could you also see towards Tolovici, Dubica, and those villages north-east?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we could see Tolovici, Jelovac, Hrasnica. Hrasnica was another Serb village and so on. Yes, you could see quite a lot from up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that to the north and north-east of you, there were Serb villages, and at a slightly higher altitude than yours?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time the Serbs had already left, so who filled in this space?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was mostly an empty space because the Serbs had just left, and some Serbs had stayed behind, not all of them left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did then, into this empty space, move citizens of either Croat or Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody was moving in yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that one of predominant features or rather the dominant hill in case of any conflict in the vicinity of your village was a hill called Jelovac?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who was on Jelovac at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is near Muslim villages so Muslims were on Jelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they have some guards on duty there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess so, yes. They must have had their organised village guards too. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when you reached Ravni Put, how many men were there during the first hour or so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that more than 30 villagers turned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And families, were they --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They stayed at home because we did not know what was going on or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there was no gunfire. There was no shooting in your village, was there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some fire from Jelovac, from that dominant feature. As soon as we arrived there, I did not get there later than 7.00 and yet fire had already been open on Ravni Put from Jelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you mean that the first shots were fired at you around 7.00?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. But when I got there, it was when it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So what did you decide, that there were so many of you, your village guards there at that place, and what was your conclusion? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at first we were completely at sea. We simply didn't know what was going on. When we did eventually realise, then we tried to organise ourselves, although it was difficult because they were all villagers and there were elderly people among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when was it that morning that you concluded, that you decided that there might also be an infantry attack on your village by the army?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because they had already opened fire on our village and people were already coming to Jelovac, and in the village of Hrasnica because one can see it too, and that is why we decided that there could be an infantry attack even though we could not be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Nobody told you that, it is something that you concluded yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, that morning -- no, let us rephrase it. Were there any people in your village who -- men, then, went to join shifts in the fighting against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: They were members of the HVO, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They volunteered to join the shifts against Serbs. I wasn't really much interested in all that so I don't know much about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't know perhaps any details about the organisation, but they went as Croats, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And any of those people who took shifts beforehand, were any of them in the village on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, because it wasn't their turn, so most of them were in their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the armament of all the men in the village was roughly what we already talked about, it had not improved, or had it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from those shifts, yes, we had some automatic weapons, but those were merely M-48s, hunting rifles, drum rifles. But most people usually bought rifles. Serbs, when they were leaving, they were selling them, I suppose in order to get some money, so that people were buying them from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. So you told us that the gunfire started. Could you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. describe in two or three sentences that first day what happened? How did the conflict unfold as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at first we were all confused because we didn't know what or how or who. In the morning, the fire was sporadic. There were no infantry attacks, direct attacks. But we sought shelter behind houses and wondered what to do. And then we agreed to -- in the direction of Strbac, of Jardol, that the villagers who were there, who were nearer there, that we should pick out some elevated points and then take them. And Strbci [phoen], Babici, Potok, villagers from there stayed at home. Mostly people were at -- in their respective homes, and that was the so-called front line but it was a far cry from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is you selected some natural spots from which men or groups of men could defend the houses in case of the attack from any side on the village?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But did also the cannon fire start that day?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that day, from the village of Bukve and we later on heard it was BOFOR 40-millimetres it also opened fire on the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, what is BOFORS?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: BOFORS is an anti-aircraft gun, 40 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But it can also fire horizontally, it need not fire only vertically towards aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that day it was firing horizontally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did that piece of weapon cause any concrete damage? Could one see the marks?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it destroyed houses, by and large. There were no wounded or killed yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How did that day end in terms of warfare? How would you sum up the day?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the evening -- rather, in the late afternoon, it all ended, it all stopped, it all came to a halt as if an agreement had been reached. And we just gathered and talked and discussed that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You suffered no casualties in the village.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That day, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To be quite clear, did you ever return the fire? And if you did, then targeting what?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't with hunting rifles because Jelovac is quite far away, I mean, for a hunting rifle. So we didn't really return the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the other side did not try to send its infantry into the village?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. What happened the next day, on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the gunfire was intensified, and then infantry men entered Strbac and killed two men who were in houses. They killed that one who volunteered to fight against the Serbs, he was at home, the one who was taking shifts up there. And he took the road above us. He wasn't on the front line or anything. But they had just entered behind those houses, and I heard that a man opened a burst of fire from a hill and simply mowed him down. The other one was standing next to a cowshed, and as he was standing by that wooden cowshed, the other one opened fire and just killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of those men, nicknames or something?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one of them was my school fellow. He was called Dragan Babic, Crni, and another one was -- well, we called him Hristo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there any civilians killed that day?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was anybody wounded that day?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were a couple of bullets, yes. But I wouldn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When they conquered that part of the village, that small part of the village, how did you respond?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we then started to climb down, because Kosanica is the most exposed part, so that we ran down to help people expel them from there. It was then that we established some sort of a front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where did the ABiH members retreat?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were already in Hrasnica, in that Serb village. They had gone down to Grabak, to Serb houses. And we were in our own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that on that second day, the BH army filled in the void in those Serb villages north of your village?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the second or third day, it was all filled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How did the situation unfold the next day, on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the fire continued to gain in intensity, but then we had already organised ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have any wounded or killed again?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, quite a number. In a year we had 33 fatalities, and about 50 per cent of us were wounded once or several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did members of the BH army ever manage to take your village?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never, except on the 1st of September, when they brought tanks in. Some of them entered our trenches but we managed to repel them, and we maintained this front line throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But that was later.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, September, that was their fiercest offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of minor questions about those early days of the conflict until about the 20th of April. When did you consolidate your front line? When could you say that you consolidated your line, held it fast until the end of the war, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what shall I tell you? In the beginning it wasn't really a proper front line until we dug in because, every day, one or two of us were killed. So we simply had to dig in in order to make a proper front line, so as to stay alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Without going back to it, but nevertheless we have to mention it, you mentioned the offensive. Is it correct that in 1993 you experienced two really fierce offensives?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Although there were attacks practically day in, day out.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was practically almost every day. There were some attacks every day, day in and day out, but these two were really fierce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But as a rule, there were no attacks at night in the first part of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at first. But later on those attacks were the worst. There were subversive groups that would attack at night, at midnight or 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You already mentioned those offensives which came later, in September, in early September. But there was another one before it. Could you tell us when?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That offensive on your village -- rather, the objective of the offensive, was it your village, or was it part of some bigger plan?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose our village was of particular interest for it because it was adjacent to Mahala, so it represented an access to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps on the map that you have there you could show us that position. So your village, and then will you draw with the pointer towards Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's like that, and then to Kruscica, and there it bifurcates, it branches off into two parts. So we would have been cut off and I don't think we would have managed to stand ground. I think that would have been the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But just to explain it to the Chamber, which forces were in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I mean, whose troops were in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the Muslims were in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean the BH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Whose forces controlled Mahala, which you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Had that operation succeeded, what would have happened in that sector?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that that would have been the end of Vitez. I think there would have been quite a massacre there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In that second offensive, tanks also took part in the fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You personally, how many tanks did you see in the area in which you were fighting?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In my sector, there were three tanks. We managed to destroy two; one survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One survived. Could you tell us, perhaps, how far did the tanks get, how near you they were?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were over our trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean over your trench, literally?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, literally over our trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it a conventional army attack, with infantry following the tanks?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you managed to push them off?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, Mr. Marjanovic, the following: On the 16th of April, as an inhabitant of the village, you took part in the defence of the village, did you not? What was your motive for doing so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my motive was to safeguard and defend my wife, my children, the village, and the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So defend your home, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that particular moment, when you started to do this, did anybody mobilise you? Orally or in written form, did anybody say that you were a soldier belonging to such and such a unit, or that you were a soldier, quite simply?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that came later. Not in those first days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you received information of this kind?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I became commander of the sector - I was injured that day - on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the 20th. Let's stay with that date. What kind of information did you receive that day?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was told by Anto Bertovic that I was being appointed commander of the sector of the village of Krcevine, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a written order to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you were wounded on that day. Was that before you were appointed commander or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I returned that day in the evening from having my wound tended to, and when I came home, Bertovic came and appointed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: They didn't keep you on in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was allowed to return home straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at that time in 1993 there were some other units in Vitez, predominantly of Croat composition?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean other units?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, other units.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of those other units? For example, the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never a member of these groups, special purpose groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When Bertovic came, or the next day when you got a written appointment and were deployed as commander of the region and were wounded, from that day on, did you consider yourself to be a member of a military unit of any kind -- actually, the military unit of which you became the commander?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that became clear to me only at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that you became a member of the Vitez Brigade on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, did you ever fight in any other locality apart from your own village?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who else was within the composition of that unit which was now formalised? Was it you yourself who was mobilised alone, or were there others?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we were all mobilised. All the military-able men in the village of Krcevine were mobilised. And everybody who was over the age of 60, we formed labour platoons for us to be able to entrench ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it, then, true that every military-able man in the village was given his wartime assignment, whether work duties in military platoons or a military assignment?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So if they were military-able men, young men, they would become members of your unit which was located in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you had an area of responsibility, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to point it out on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: From Jardol, there is a stream called Brezovac. From that place right up to this spot, Krizancevo Selo, where there's another stream, Tolovicki Potok, and that was my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we take it, then, that you had the area from the stream to the west, to the stream to the east of your village?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in that locality, there are some roads, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are several roads leading to Hrasnica and thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: They are roads leading from the north towards the main road in the valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it was your task to block those roads, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After the beginning of the war, at any point did you obtain reinforcements? Did members of other units come to reinforce your defence line?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, during stronger attacks when our line came under heavy attack, then we would get reinforcements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you, as the commander of the area, you sought reinforcements, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an example, when once you received these reinforcements, once you were helped out by other units, for example, what was that like and what unit was it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually they were the Munja units which were in Buhine Kuce. They came to us and we would deploy them. We would have a local man with one of the members of this other unit because they didn't know the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some of them were from Vitez and others were from Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they include the remnants of the HVO brigade in Zenica and Travnik which had disintegrated?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you exactly because I didn't know them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. But at all events, once they came to your locality, whom did they report to?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So their officer, commanding officer would report to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you would then deploy them in your locality where you needed them to help out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Krcni [phoen], in my area, I was responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did they accept your orders?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, although it wasn't a real army yet but there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, under the circumstances, did it ever happen that anybody refused to carry out your orders?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But let us take a hypothetical situation. Had somebody refused to carry out your orders, did you have any way in compelling them to follow your orders?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I tell Anto Bertovic because he was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If reinforcements came to the front line without reporting to you, hypothetically speaking, what would your relationship be?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean if reinforcements came?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have cases of that type. It would depend. During the worst situations when two or three of our men were killed and had quite a number of wounded, we would try and cover the area and ask for reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How long would the reinforcements stay?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would stay three or four days and then go back; during the offensive, while the offensive lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that they would stay until your defence had been consolidated? Could we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that your area of responsibility ended in the vicinity of Buhine Kuce and there was heavy fighting around Buhine Kuce, was there not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly. I think the people from Krizancevo Selo would be able to tell you that better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did your men, as it was to your flank wing that took part in the fighting around Buhine Kuce?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No because we were under attack at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now return to the beginning of the conflict for a moment and focus on that. You said that there were 15 Muslim households in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What happened to those families, those households?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were -- went on living quite normally in their houses for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did anyone wish to evict them from their homes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did anybody maltreat them?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you use them for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were their houses burnt?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, their houses were not burnt, and they've all now returned to their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When they left, were they given any explanation and how did they come to leave; could you describe that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they asked me, "Marinko, do you know how long that will last?" And I said, "Well, I'd like it to last as short as possible." "Well," they said, "if it doesn't last too long, perhaps we could stay." And I said, "Well, it's better that you stay." And when 15 or 20 days had passed, they came to me again and asked me again and asked me again. And as they were all behind our backs, nobody had heard anything, and the fighting was at the top of the village and they asked me whether they could be transferred to Zenica where there was a majority Muslim population. I said that I would have to ask. I asked Anto Bertovic and he said that they could go of their own free will if they wanted to themselves but not us to make them go. And that's what I told them. They thanked me, and they left their property with the locals to look after. What they could take with them in their cars they took. They got into their cars and went safely to Zenica, and nothing happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have those people come back; did they come back?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Today, you mean, are they back today? Yes, all of them came back except for the ones that left for Australia or America.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And they've taken up residence in their own houses, have they?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During the war, were any of your Croatian houses destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some of our houses, 15 to 20 were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This happened during the conflict with inflammatory bullets, and when the tank entered our village. They set fire to these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier on, and let's just go back to that point for a second and recapitulate: Your losses, your casualties, how many of your HVO soldiers lost their lives in the village during all these events?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: 33 fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How many people were wounded, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: About 20 civilians were wounded, and up at the front line, 50 per cent of us actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, if I understand you correctly in your descriptions of the situation, in the circumstances, would it be true to say that the enemy army was always in front of you on the other side of the defence line?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in front of us and above us. They were on an elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And at any given time, your village and your houses, including the 15 Muslim houses, were in the rear behind your backs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At any time during the war, did you take -- were you in a situation or take part in an operation which this relationship was changed in any way with the enemy in front and above?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we always maintained that same defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The enemy was in front of you, as you said. Were there any civilian targets where the BH army portions?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So all the positions taken up by the army were outside Muslim villages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is to say they were on hills, by rivers and so on. There was no built-up area?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have to use your weapons to destroy any of their features?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Their premises. So along those lines, I assume they had trenches like you did, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had dug in too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Kordic has no questions to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, I only recently had your summary of evidence and I wasn't expecting you to come until later in the week so though I have some questions to ask you, they may be a bit disconnected; I apologise. Tell us, please, why did the Muslims attack you in your village? What had you done to deserve it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had no dealings with the local political or military leadership; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the days themselves, that's the 16th, 17th, and 18th, you were located in your own village; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You didn't see anything of what was happening in Vitez or indeed the short distance further east in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to those matters in detail, can the witness see, very briefly, that Exhibit 653 again. Now, you've told us that there was no organisation save by village guards before the troubles took the form they did. We've got this document. It's dated, as you'll notice, the 14th of April, so it's before the conflict. It's headed the Viteska Brigade, and it's said to be a list of the personnel from the 1st Battalion of the Vitez or Viteska Brigade by their deployment. When we come to your village, which we'll see towards the bottom of the page under the heading, do you see it there, 3rd Company, Commander Ivica Drmic, and under Krcevine there are 20 soldiers. Now, can you just please explain what you understand the position of those 20 soldiers to be.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could explain that, yes. Those 20 soldiers took shifts against the Serbs. That's how many there were in Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How do you mean that's how many there were; how many soldiers there were or how many village guards there were or how many members of the Viteska Brigade? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were just the locals of Krcevine which went up in shifts against the Serbs at Slatka Vode and places like that. They took their turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you one of them or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, were you working at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have a job at the time? On the 14th of April, did you have a job?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't have a job. I was about town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. But so that we can understand it, because we've had a number of explanations for these entries on this bit of paper, I'll go through some of them possibly with you, but there are 20 people who would go, you would say, on shifts. And then in addition to that, there are the village guards, are there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were also members of the village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. So that you would say that the village guards are drawn from these 20 people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It was mostly local people and they -- when they were off duty, when they were not at the front lines, they could join the village guards. They could volunteer. It wasn't mandatory but they could do so if they wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. But these 20 men or these 20 soldiers, they were identified in some way, were they, as people who were prepared to go to the front line?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They volunteered to go. We could have gone if we had wanted to, to the front line against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when they went to the front line, who came and organised them; was it Ivica Drmic of the 3rd Company of the Viteska Brigade? Is that what happened, he turned up and took them along to the front line? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a member, and I didn't know who took them off to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You seem to have some knowledge of what they were doing. What was the organisation of these people in your very small village, please, that made them front line volunteers and left you man-about-town, village guard? Can you explain it for us?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can explain, but I wasn't interested in the war which is why I was not a member. If I had wanted to go and fight against the Serbs, I could have done so. But I didn't. So I don't know how they went, when they went, when they came back, who took them there. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were aware, of course, of the existence of organised soldiers in Vitez, the Viteska Brigade, yes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's deal with a little bit of geography next and I think that the map D88/2 will probably be more useful than the present map for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a map that is also produced in the Vitez binder but I'm using the Defence exhibit number from now on, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we can leave it at that sort of magnification for the time being, and then we'll focus on bits of detail in a second or so. This map shows more clearly than the other map that there are, in fact, two main roads, two substantial roads going from south-east to north-west, or east to west, as the road that runs through Vitez itself. And then in an arc above it, there is another quite substantial road. In fact, I think it's the road that now has the large shopping centres and things like that on it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see that to the north of the river, apart from a few houses on the road that leads up to Krcevine, there are no houses possibly because the river floods or something like that, I don't know, but there is an area with no houses on it between the two roads; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean this part here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if we can, let's focus on Vitez itself, if we can get down to a little bit closer to Vitez itself, that's fine. We've been using, in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this trial, for part of Vitez the term "old" or Stari Vitez, and we've also been using the term "the Mahala" for Vitez. Now, are those two terms describing the same area or are they terms that refer to different areas?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's all the same area, Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or the Mahala; we can use either term.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it's been called for centuries, Mahala and Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if we go in a little closer, just a teeny bit closer if we could, and more again if it's possible, we can see there, if we can focus on it, the fire station, which is shown on the south side of the road leading out of Vitez to the west. That fire station, broadly speaking, marks the beginning of the area of the Mahala or Stari Vitez, is that correct, which lies to the west of it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Well, you tell me. Does Stari Vitez start further to the east of that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The fire station is right in the middle of Mahala. Where Stari Vitez begins, well, that's all the same area. It's just a different name for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. So we can consider an area on either side of the fire station as being Stari Vitez. Very well. Now, you've described going home on the night of the 15th, the early hours of the morning of the 16th. You say you went from Vitez, from a discotheque, and you went over the bridge to your village of Krcevine. Now, is it this road that you're describing, going along by the fire station, and then turning right at the next road that we can see and going over the river?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have one correction to make. The fire station is in the middle of Mahala and not Stari Vitez. I passed by there and crossed the bridge and went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You go up the road, turn right, over the river, and then over the next road that's a little further to the north and into your village; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we stay with this map and now come out, if the technical booth can help us, and we'll go further north on the map. Perhaps the usher could help or someone. We need to draw back a little bit. And then go a little further -- we want to go a bit further north, really, right up to the top of the map, I think, really. Thank you very much. We can now see, and perhaps we should focus in a little bit until the words become clearer, we can see the village. Focus in a bit. That's fine. Thank you very much. Perhaps if you can move the map just a touch to the left -- no, the other way. I always get it wrong. There it is. Right. That shows your village, and above it, slightly out of focus, is Grabak. And then above that and slightly to the left is Hrasnica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Jelovac, the hill there where you say there was a Muslim attack, is not marked on the map, but I think it's in this area; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we can see is that your village lies immediately beside the northern of the two roads that pass either through or beside Vitez, doesn't it? It lies immediately beside that road.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But there is, in fact, a distance, we can see roughly what it is, we can see that the area of land between the two roads at about the area of your village is a little under a kilometre, 700 or 800 metres, I suppose, from one road to the other, with very few houses on it. You say that the attack on your village related to the Mahala or Stari Vitez. Is that just a guess, or is that a matter of information?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The offensive? You mean the offensive to join those areas?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the offensive on your village that you've described by the BiH. As I understood your evidence, you say that that was connected with --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I concluded that because they attacked us every day. They attacked us. Why would they attack us but in order to link up with Mahala and to cut us off? It's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the road itself, this northern road, who had control of that road during this part of the fighting? Because it's a main road capable of taking large vehicles. Who controlled that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean this main road, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Who controlled that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no one controlled it. Both the Muslims and the Croats could fire at it. It was within their firing range.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it occur to you - I'm not advancing this as a proposition, I'm just inquiring - did it occur to you that the interest in your village may have had rather more to do with gaining control of that road? Because your village had sight of that road, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no chance of that. They wanted to link up with Mahala. They were not interested in the road. They controlled a part of the road at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The part of the road that they controlled at Grbavica is the other road, that is, the southern of the two roads, and it's just by Divjak, isn't it, or it's to the east of Divjak?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. That's the same road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't know that there's a great deal of point debating these matters with these witnesses. They seem to find the questions very difficult. I don't understand why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question on this topic is this: Were there Croat snipers working in and from your village, please?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Can you give me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Mr. Marjanovic, we're trying to find out where a place called Krizancevo Selo is. You say it's a hill near you; is that right? Near your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's the village right next to Krcevine, on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the village next to Krcevine, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it go by another name?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Krizancevo Selo or Dubravica. That's where the massacres happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall, and we can see on this map - if we come out again, we'll just be able to link this to the other map - we can see right on the right-hand corner of this map, Dubravica in the bottom right-hand corner. To connect this with the evidence of the last witness, the very right-hand road running approximately north, slightly north-east, is the road that goes off to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man Beso of whom you speak - I'm not able to deal with the detail of what you say one way or another at the moment; possibly I shan't be able to deal with it before you leave the witness box - but the man Beso, you say, was by the fire station at some time after midnight on the turn of the night, 15th/16th; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You simply saw him there with a group of other men.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were with how many other men in your car?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They tried to stop you, you say. What was the apparent purpose of stopping you, if it happened?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. In fact, they didn't stop me. I don't know what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So there was simply a group of men, they made as if to stop you, but somebody knew you, the man Beso, and you were waved on.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I knew Beso well. We were good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with that in detail this afternoon if I have time, but I didn't know of the name of the witness until lunchtime -- the name of Beso until lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following morning, you tell us that you were awakened, I think, by the sounds coming from Ravni, which is a part of your village. What time do you say that was?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The fire was heard first from Jelovac that morning, not from Grabak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What time do you say that was?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 6.00 or 7.00 a.m. Not later than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we just look at your summary, please. Did you prepare this printed summary that we have? Perhaps you'd like to have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps he could have it in the original language, or in his language, rather. Paragraph 3.3 is what I'm going to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may provide a copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.3, please: "On 16 April 1993, the shooting had awakened me and I went on Ravni Put (a part of the village). The village residents made an earlier agreement that Ravni Put would be the meeting point in case of an attack. There, I met the other Croats from the village, while the women stayed in the houses." The next paragraph is 3.4: "We established the defence line on Ravni Put because we estimated that the ABiH would try an infantry attack on the village. We had some weapons borrowed from the shift members who have not been at that time on the defence line ... some people had their own weapons ..." Then paragraph 3.5: "During the whole day, the ABiH forces were taking an offensive action on Krcevine and nearby Grabak using small arms," and then you say, "and artillery ..." Now, you don't, there, set out anything about a start time for this alleged attack. But you do make it clear that you first of all had a chance to go and deal with the defence line on Ravni Put. Think back, please. What was the earliest time your village was, in fact, under any attack at all on that day, assuming it was?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Early in the morning, between 6.00 and 7.00 a.m., the attack started from Jelovac. There was sporadic shooting on Ravni Put and the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, unless I'm shown contemporaneous documentation, and I may well be, but unless I'm shown contemporaneous documentation about this, I'm going to challenge this from you and I'm going to suggest you've put that time rather early for any attack. Now, think back, please. Did you not have time to deal with your defence line and so on before any attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have time. We didn't organise anything. We didn't know it was going to happen. And that was exactly when the attack started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, you see, you couldn't see Ahmici from your village, could you, because you've got the hill that runs through Sivrino Selo and so on in between. But did you hear the shooting that was going on in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ahmici is much further away from my village. It's not just a hill that's between these villages; otherwise, I would have had to hear the shooting. But my village is quite far from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, well, your village is about six kilometres from Ahmici, as the crow flies. Did you hear any gunfire from any other places further east of your village before, as you say, you were attacked?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I was going along Krcevine, I heard them shooting from Tolovici towards Krizancevo Selo. But I was focusing on my own village, I didn't have time to look around too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the fighting or the gunfire that was coming, as you would say, from Hrasnica, did you see people going there in advance to prepare themselves to attack you? Did you see any movement of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't see that because I was asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you ever been told of the movement of vehicles in preparation for this alleged attack on you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that I learned about it in the morning. I had no idea about the Muslim attack on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question is quite specific. Has anybody told you of vehicles rolling up into the village of Hrasnica the night before in order to prepare an attack on you, please?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was in Vitez, in the disco. Nobody said anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, there are various routes, no doubt, back routes and so on, to Hrasnica. But is one way to that village through your village of Grabak, or can't you reach Hrasnica through your village in Grabak.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: There are two roads, not one. One goes through Grabak and another goes through Hrasnica. They go towards Preocica, Zenica, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. So are we to take it, please, that the attack that came on you, as you describe it, was mounted with the weapons that already happened to be Hrasnica that night. There was no question of there being prepared reinforcements, was there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know whether they prepared or not. I just know that they opened fire in the morning between 6.00 and 7.00 a.m., they fired on Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that if there was any firing that morning at all, it followed the attack that Croats had already mounted in other parts of this locality of yours, and was reactive to it, i.e., it followed the attacks that you heard elsewhere. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How do you know that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know because the Muslims fired on our village and what happened before that I have no idea, or whether anything happened before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You describe the Stari Vitez as being in the possession of the Muslims, do you remember telling us that, or under the control of the Muslims? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was during the war but there were also Croats in Mahala before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember telling us that it was the Muslims who controlled Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember the truck bomb incident? You probably heard it from your village, it's only a kilometre away. Do you remember the truck bomb incident?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You must have learned about what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: We just heard rumours. We didn't have any exact information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What rumours did you hear?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that a system had exploded in Mahala; it was all rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Now, thinking back, do you think that the description of the Muslims having control of the Mahala is fair or do you think it's rather more a question of the fact that the Croats had them surrounded and they were confined within the Mahala? Which was it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be better to say that we were all surrounded by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking about the Mahala. Were they in control of it or were they simply surrounded by Croats and kept in a small enclave? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my judgement, later on, they were surrounded. But before that, they controlled Mahala, and it's nearly half of Vitez. They controlled Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Muslims from your village at some point were free to simply get into their cars and drive presumably over the mountains to Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was because there was, of course, a rise and fall in the level of aggression from time to time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. I know that they were with us for more than a month, they had contacts with us. And there were no problems although we were being attacked from the other side, from up there, but they condemned this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Somehow or another, these people were able to travel by car. They would hardly be travelling by car to Zenica if there was active fighting going on on the road between Zenica and Vitez, would they, it's pretty obvious?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were checkpoints, but we promised them that no one would hinder them or provoke them, and that's how it was. They asked me for free passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were you able to sign passes for these people? Did you have that much authority given to you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, who signed the passes then, Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There were no passes at all. We simply talked to the men and agreed this. We told them to let them through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, was that freedom of movement granted to the people encircled in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question very well. They could go around freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the people from Stari Vitez in a position simply to up sticks, as the vernacular has it in our language, get in their cars, and drive to Zenica or were they kept in Stari Vitez? Which is it, please?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say because I was in Krcevine for a whole year. I never went down there since after the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I probably have finished. There is a number of documents that might have been raised with this witness. Can I just consider them for a minute, and if I'm satisfied that I needn't put any of them, then I'll probably have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I could sit down to do it rather than stand to do it. Thank you. Your Honour, I'm not going to produce documents of marginal value and simply repeat categories of documents we've seen before. The only reason I'm putting in documents about service with different categories of witnesses is to ensure that a full and fair picture is presented given the answers being advanced about membership of the various -- therefore I'll put the one comment to the witness for his comments. 1473.11, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a document that we have setting out your service, I think. You are Marinko, son of Screcko Marjanovic, born in 1967; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This describes you as having been a military conscript and a member of the 92nd home defence regiment Viteska in the period 15th of November 1991 to the 30th of March 1996, performing the duties of company commander until the mobilisation signed by Colonel Dragan Vinjac. Do you agree with that as a description of your military service?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, but it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what way is this document not true, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't from 1991, it was from 1993. I joined only when the conflict broke out. So 1991 is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your explanation for this document which seems quite specific about its date, 15th of November, 1991, how can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what can I say? I think it's largely for those shares, those worthless shares that we got. To prolong our service so as to get more of those shares, but when we got them, they were completely worthless and this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other question. The front line at Krcevine was roughly how long? Are we dealing in a front line of 500 metres, a kilometre, what?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly two kilometres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in August of 1993, where were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Which month did you say; I'm not quite sure about these new names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, August 1993. Well, I was in Krcevine, wasn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were the commander in charge of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as the 20th or about -- the 20th of April, that is. Not March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 8th of August, therefore, you were in your village and you were the commander.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: 8th of August, 1993, you say? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember the visit to your front line by Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Kordic did not come to my front line during that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've had evidence of his being seen there with military commanders, including Mr. Cerkez. Now, thinking back, do you remember a visit by Mr. Cerkez to your front line?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions, yes, Mr. Cerkez would drop by our front line, but I did not see Dario Kordic unless he was with my deputy commander and he did not report it to me, but I simply have no recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What is the name of your deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Anto Radalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see Kordic anywhere else other than in your village?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know him at all?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not personally. I knew he was a politician and that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see him in military uniform ever?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. And you have no recollection of seeing him in your village in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your deputy, is he still living in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He does live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it's ten past 4 o’clock. Are you going to be many minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Maximum five, worst case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I put that to the interpreters, worst case five minutes, can we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us about the massacre in Krizancevo Selo. Will you tell us what that massacre was. Who committed it? What was it about?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The massacrers perpetrated the massacre against the Croat population. They killed 104 individuals that day. A number of individuals were taken away and then killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it happened late in 1992, early 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite a number of civilians were also killed on that occasion, women and children, and those captors who were -- who survived that, they were also killed later on, 104 -- well, I don't know but it was over 100 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, according to the translation, you said that it happened late in 1992, early 1993. I thought the evidence was that it was late 1993. Why don't we ask the witness. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was late 1993, as far as I can remember, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was obviously my mistake. It was the end of 1993 as the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there was also fighting there in the very beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was fighting in Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I got the years mixed up. Was there any fighting in early 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For a year, the conflict broke out at the same time that it did in our case and it is a neighbouring village and it lasted just as long as it did in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, in early 1994 there was. You mentioned that Beso, did you mean Beso Ahmet who was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he lived in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Kruscica, you say. Thank you. There was mention about the siege, about the encirclement, and perhaps it may be the question of the -- what comes first, the hen or the egg, but will you please tell us, would you agree that the Lasva Valley, the part that you were in, Krcevine, and the environs of Vitez was encircled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you would also agree that within that -- that inside that circle, there were parts where that same BH army was encircled too?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
